extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students studying patent validity and prior-use defenses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent novelty and the defense of prior use in patent litigation, covering burden/standard of proof, admissible evidence, identity tests, public use, dates of invention, and special rules for combinations and documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent as prima facie evidence of novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: That the patent itself is prima facie evidence of the novelty of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a patent is in evidence the burden of proof rests on the defendant to show want of novelty; courts treat the patent as prima facie proof that the invention was new (examples and cases cited: Byerly v. Cleveland Seed Oil Works; Shaver v. Skinner Mfg. Co.). The weight of the patent as evidence may be aided by showing that the invention was subjected to rigid scrutiny and comparison in the Patent Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal novelty defeated by prior use, prior patent, or prior publication
rubrics_metrics.description: That legal novelty cannot exist where there was either prior use, prior patent, or prior publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An affirmative showing of any of these is equivalent to a denial of legal novelty. The defendant must prove at least one of them beyond a reasonable doubt (numerous case citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part test for prior-use defense (identity and public accessibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior-use defence is further divisible into two points: (1) whether the art or article alleged to have been previously used was identical with the patented invention; (2) whether the use alleged was such as to have rendered the invention accessible to the public at the date of the plaintiff's conception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both points require conclusive evidence. Identity may be established by specimens, descriptions, or expert inspection; accessibility requires the invention to have been complete, operative, and publicly used so as to disclose its character, construction, and mode of operation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: That the defendant must prove want of novelty/prior use beyond a reasonable doubt; every reasonable doubt as to prior use must be resolved in favor of the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple citations emphasize that prior use is a question of fact and the defendant bears the burden; mere preponderance or single unreliable witness testimony is insufficient. The defendant should exhaust testimony and fix dates as early as evidence permits because new evidence is not allowed after plaintiff's rebuttal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and weight of admissible evidence for identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity of the prior article with the patented invention may be established by specimens, descriptions (written/printed), prior patents/applications, models, witnesses, and expert inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specimens are the most reliable; when specimens exist but are under defendant control, failure to present them raises a strong presumption against identity. Descriptions and rejected applications are admissible to show characteristics but are weaker for proving operativeness. Models and Patent Office records can be strong evidence. File wrappers, caveats, and rejected applications have limits (e.g., not conclusive of reduction to practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specimens and models preferred; failure to produce harms defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: When specimens of the alleged anticipating invention exist and are under the defendant's control, his failure to present them raises a strong presumption against their identity with the patented article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts give highest weight to existing specimens or models (Morris v. Barrett). If defendant possesses alleged prior articles but does not produce them, presumption is strongly against him (Bailey Washing & Wringing Mach. Co. v. Lincoln).

rubrics_metrics.name: Witness testimony reliability and effect of lapse of time
rubrics_metrics.description: The testimony of witnesses who speak from personal recollection only is of comparatively little value; its weight diminishes with remoteness and complexity of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence must be positive and specific, not conjectural or indefinite. Indefinite recollections after many years, without models, are unreliable. Courts resolve doubts in favor of patent holder when witness memory is inconsistent with other events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documents and publications: admissibility and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions, printed or written, patents, applications, circulars, and catalogues may be admitted to show essential characteristics or prior use, but writings alone generally do not prove reduction to practice or operativeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A circular published by a person claiming the invention was new may outweigh parol evidence. Catalogues and printed matter may show prior use (Forschner v. Bauchgarten). Rejected applications and caveats are not conclusive evidence of reduction to practice; file wrappers are generally hearsay for reduction-to-practice issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public and practical use requirement (including territorial limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of an invention renders it accessible to the public only when the invention is complete, operative, and practically used in such a manner as to disclose its character, construction, and mode of operation to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such use must have occurred in the United States to defeat a domestic patent; foreign uses generally do not invalidate a U.S. patent unless they gave public knowledge in the U.S. A single established public use is sufficient unless the knowledge was extinguished or the art became a lost art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior use must be complete, operative, and capable of producing claimed result
rubrics_metrics.description: Sufficient prior use must show that the device was complete, capable of producing some result and was known in the country; mere existence of a device capable of such use is not enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof should show the device would accomplish what is claimed (Sayles v. Chicago & Northwestern Ry. Co.). Descriptions, sketches, and drawings alone are generally insufficient to show operativeness or practical use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents: prior-use defence must show prior use of entire combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A defence to a patent for a combination as a whole must apply to the entire combination and not to its separate parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use of individual elements does not invalidate a combination patent unless the entire combination was previously known and used (Bates v. Coe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of similar but not identical prior devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior use of articles less perfect but identical in principle invalidates the patent; prior use of similar but not identical devices cannot defeat the patent but may show the state of the art and limit the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior devices embody the same principles and can produce the same result, the defence will prevail (Stitt v. Fastem R. B. Co.). Similar devices may restrict claim scope but not necessarily destroy novelty (Magin v. McKay; McFarland v. Spencer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity vs equivalence as factual question for experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether one thing is identical with or the 'equivalent' of another is a question of fact, often for expert inspection of the inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts rely on expert testimony and inspection where identity is not apparent on inspection; if identity can only be known by actual use, the defendant should prove actual use. Evidence of what might have been done with prior machines is speculative and inadmissible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dates of invention and effect of applications/earlier patents
rubrics_metrics.description: The date of the plaintiff's patent is prima facie the date of his inventive act; the date of filing an application (if accompanying the patent) is prima facie the date of the inventive act; an issued reissue or extension may relate back to earlier dates in certain circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If defendant shows knowledge or use prior to application or patent, the burden shifts to plaintiff to prove earlier conception and reduction to practice. Records of the Patent Office fix application dates — parol evidence cannot substitute. An original patent may carry the date of original discovery in some cases (Consolidated Bunging Apparatus Co. v. Woerlo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural limits on evidence and rebuttal (exhaustion rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: New evidence for the defendant is not allowed after the plaintiff's rebutter; defendant must exhaust his testimony on remoteness and dates when making his defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because defendant is not allowed to reproduce evidence after rebuttal, he must present full evidence of prior use and its date during his initial case. Courts admonish defendants to fix dates as early as their evidence permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of employer/license facts and inconsistent conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence that the defendant or witnesses accepted licenses from the patentee, sought other inventions, or offered large sums inconsistent with claimed prior use may overcome prior-use assertions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff may show inconsistent acts (e.g., seeking license from patentee, later patenting similar devices) to rebut defendant's claim of prior use. Witness statements contradicted by documentary or circumstantial evidence lose weight.
